title: Can attention grow?
hook: after a three-month retreat, meditators improved at fine visual attention tasks (MacLean et al.)

segments.voice: Yesterday, two kinds of attention: focused attention on one object, and open monitoring of whatever arises. Your line was focus, then open.

A piano tuner leans in, strikes a key, and hears that it's a hair flat. To an untrained ear it sounds fine. A birder hears three notes in a hedge and names the bird without seeing it. That kind of hearing is learned. So here's the question William James left open when he said this ideal was easier to define than to train: can attention itself be trained like an ear, not just used but made sharper? Today, one study that tried to find out.
screen: `A KEY A HAIR FLAT.` → `EARS GET TRAINED.` → `CAN ATTENTION?`

segments.voice: A team led by the psychologist Katherine MacLean studied people on an intensive three-month meditation retreat, with long hours of practice each day, much of it focused attention on the breath. A comparison group waited to do the same retreat later. Before, during and after, both groups did a demanding visual task: lines flashed up one after another, and the job was to catch the rare line slightly shorter than the rest. It's dull, and that's the point. It tests whether attention can stay sharp and steady over time. The result: the retreat group got better at telling the short lines from the long ones, and better at staying sharp as the task wore on. When the comparison group later did its own retreat, it showed gains too. So the honest answer, at least from this study, is yes. Attention can grow. Now the honest limits. This was an intensive retreat, not a few minutes before work. The task was a lab task, not a whole life. And one study needs others to agree with it. But it points somewhere: at least the kind of attention this task measured isn't simply fixed. It responded to practice, the way a tuner's ear does, a lab looking from the outside at something meditators talk about from the inside.
screen: `A RETREAT, AND A GROUP THAT WAITED.` · `CATCH THE SLIGHTLY SHORTER LINE.` · `SHARPER, AND STEADIER.` · `ONE STUDY, HONEST LIMITS.`

segments.voice: Rest on the breath at the nostrils and make the task finer than usual: notice the exact moment each in-breath begins, the moment it turns, and the moment it ends. When you miss one, no matter; catch the next.
Can attention grow? In one careful study of a long retreat, meditators got sharper and steadier at a demanding attention task. Today's word.
Your line: it can grow. A slip isn't proof you can't, just one more rep. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Researchers test whether meditation trains attention by measuring people on demanding computer tasks before and after practice, and comparing them with a group that hasn't practiced yet.

what a scholar hears: MacLean and colleagues' retreat study, with a wait-list group that later trained too, showing gains in fine visual discrimination and sustained attention, with honest limits on how far it generalizes.
